clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of persistent hypoglycaemia in neonates and infants, driven by dysregulated insulin secretion
Most severe forms result from inactivating mutations in the KATP channel genes ABCC8 and KCNJ11, with several other genes implicated
Biochemically defined by detectable or inappropriately elevated insulin with suppressed ketones and free fatty acids during hypoglycaemia
A brisk glycaemic response to glucagon at the time of hypoglycaemia supports the diagnosis
Histology distinguishes diffuse disease affecting the whole pancreas from focal lesions confined to one region
Focal disease can be localised with specialised pancreatic imaging and potentially cured by limited surgical resection
Diazoxide is the first-line medical therapy, but KATP channel forms are frequently unresponsive and may need additional agents or surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Insulin secretion is normally gated by the beta-cell KATP channel, which closes as ATP rises to trigger release. In congenital hyperinsulinism, inactivating mutations in the channel genes ABCC8 or KCNJ11, or defects in other regulators of insulin secretion, cause the channel to remain closed, so insulin is released regardless of the prevailing glucose. Unregulated insulin drives profound hypoglycaemia and simultaneously suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis, depriving the brain of alternative fuels and creating a high risk of neurological injury. Focal disease reflects a localised somatic event superimposed on a paternally inherited mutation.
additionalDifferentials: Transient hyperinsulinism of the infant of a diabetic or growth-restricted mother
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and other overgrowth syndromes
Fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis disorders
Glycogen storage disease and other metabolic causes of hypoglycaemia
additionalInvestigations: Critical (hypoglycaemia-timed) sample for insulin, C-peptide, ketones and free fatty acids
Glucagon stimulation test at the time of hypoglycaemia to assess glycaemic response
Assessment of glucose infusion requirement to demonstrate the degree of hyperinsulinism
Molecular genetic testing of ABCC8, KCNJ11 and other hyperinsulinism genes
Specialised functional pancreatic imaging to distinguish focal from diffuse disease
redFlags: Recurrent or severe hypoglycaemia with seizures or reduced consciousness threatening brain injury
Very high glucose infusion requirements that cannot maintain normoglycaemia
Failure to respond to diazoxide, indicating likely KATP channel disease needing escalation
Signs of an underlying overgrowth or metabolic syndrome requiring broader evaluation
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on prompt prevention of hypoglycaemia to protect the brain; focal disease can be cured by targeted resection, whereas diffuse KATP channel disease is often medically resistant and may require near-total pancreatectomy with later risk of diabetes.
pitfalls: Failing to obtain a critical blood sample during hypoglycaemia, losing the key diagnostic biochemistry
Tolerating borderline glucose levels and underestimating the risk of permanent neurological damage
Assuming diazoxide will work in KATP channel disease and delaying escalation or surgery
Proceeding to extensive surgery without imaging to distinguish focal from diffuse disease
management: Provide immediate correction and prevention of hypoglycaemia with high-concentration intravenous glucose via central access and frequent or continuous enteral feeding to protect the developing brain
First-line medical therapy is diazoxide, which opens the beta-cell KATP channel, given alongside a thiazide diuretic to counter fluid retention
Add or substitute somatostatin analogues such as octreotide or long-acting lanreotide, and consider a glucagon infusion, in diazoxide-unresponsive disease
Distinguish focal from diffuse disease with specialised fluorine-18-DOPA PET pancreatic imaging, since focal lesions can be cured by limited pancreatectomy
For diffuse, medically resistant disease consider near-total pancreatectomy, accepting the later risk of diabetes and exocrine insufficiency
Monitor neurodevelopment and screen for later diabetes and exocrine pancreatic failure after surgery
Offer genetic counselling and testing of ABCC8 and KCNJ11, including parental origin to predict focal disease, and refer to a specialist congenital hyperinsulinism centre
